solution:
\(\square\)ABCD is a parallelogram, so side AB \(\parallel\) side DC and \(AB = DC\).
P is the midpoint of side AB, so \(AP = \frac{1}{2}AB\); Q is the midpoint of side DC, so \(CQ = \frac{1}{2}DC\).
Since \(AB = DC\), we get \(AP = CQ\).
Seg AP lies along side AB and seg CQ lies along side DC, and side AB \(\parallel\) side DC, so seg AP \(\parallel\) seg CQ.
In \(\square\)APCQ, the opposite sides AP and CQ are parallel and congruent.
By the test 'a quadrilateral with one pair of opposite sides parallel and congruent is a parallelogram', \(\square\)APCQ is a parallelogram.

Let \(\square\)ABCD be a rectangle. By definition every angle of a rectangle is a right angle, so \(\angle A = \angle B = \angle C = \angle D = 90^{\circ}\).
So \(\angle A \cong \angle C\) and \(\angle B \cong \angle D\), that is both pairs of opposite angles are congruent.
By the opposite angles test, a quadrilateral whose pairs of opposite angles are congruent is a parallelogram.
Hence every rectangle is a parallelogram.

Let M be the point where median DM of \(\triangle\)DEF meets side EF; then M is the midpoint of seg EF, so \(EM = MF\), and G lies on seg DM.
The point of concurrence of the medians divides each median in the ratio \(2 : 1\) from the vertex, so \(DG = 2\,GM\), that is \(GM = \frac{1}{2}DG\).
Given \(GH = DG\), so \(GM = \frac{1}{2}GH\), and since D-G-H with M between G and H, M is the midpoint of seg GH.
So in \(\square\)GEHF the diagonals are seg GH and seg EF, and both are bisected at M.
By the test 'a quadrilateral whose diagonals bisect each other is a parallelogram', \(\square\)GEHF is a parallelogram.

Let \(\square\)ABCD be a parallelogram whose angle bisectors meet in pairs at P, Q, R and S, with S the point where the bisectors of \(\angle A\) and \(\angle D\) meet.
\(\angle A\) and \(\angle D\) are adjacent angles of the parallelogram, so \(\angle A + \angle D = 180^{\circ}\).
In \(\triangle\)ASD, \(\angle SAD = \frac{1}{2}\angle A\) and \(\angle SDA = \frac{1}{2}\angle D\), so \(\angle SAD + \angle SDA = \frac{1}{2}(\angle A + \angle D) = 90^{\circ}\).
The angles of a triangle add up to \(180^{\circ}\), so \(\angle ASD = 180^{\circ} - 90^{\circ} = 90^{\circ}\), and the angle of \(\square\)PQRS at S is vertically opposite \(\angle ASD\), hence also \(90^{\circ}\).
The same argument in \(\triangle\)APB, \(\triangle\)BQC and \(\triangle\)CRD gives right angles at P, Q and R.
So all four angles of \(\square\)PQRS measure \(90^{\circ}\).
Hence \(\square\)PQRS is a rectangle.

\(\square\)ABCD is a parallelogram, so \(AB = CD\), \(BC = AD\), \(\angle A \cong \angle C\) and \(\angle B \cong \angle D\).
Given \(AP = BQ = CR = DS\).
From \(AB = CD\) and \(AP = CR\) we get \(PB = AB - AP = CD - CR = RD\).
From \(AD = BC\) and \(DS = BQ\) we get \(AS = AD - DS = BC - BQ = CQ\).
In \(\triangle\)APS and \(\triangle\)CRQ: seg AP \(\cong\) seg CR, \(\angle A \cong \angle C\) and seg AS \(\cong\) seg CQ, so \(\triangle\)APS \(\cong\) \(\triangle\)CRQ by the SAS test, giving seg PS \(\cong\) seg RQ.
In \(\triangle\)PBQ and \(\triangle\)RDS: seg PB \(\cong\) seg RD, \(\angle B \cong \angle D\) and seg BQ \(\cong\) seg DS, so \(\triangle\)PBQ \(\cong\) \(\triangle\)RDS by the SAS test, giving seg PQ \(\cong\) seg RS.
So both pairs of opposite sides of \(\square\)PQRS are congruent.
By the opposite sides test, \(\square\)PQRS is a parallelogram.
